name: Lipstick shade matching

card.summary: Choosing lipstick colour to suit skin tone and lip shape; history and safety are documented, attractiveness effects are untested.
card.note: Trace lead and PFAS have been reported in some lipsticks.

quick.overview:
Shade matching means picking a lipstick colour that suits your skin tone and lip shape. It is a removable, low-cost styling approach.

Reference sources cover lipstick history and composition; no studies of shade choice and attractiveness were found.
quick.mechanism: Colour and finish change lip contrast and apparent size: matte formulas contain more fillers, glossy ones more oil, and shimmer uses mica or pearl particles.
quick.risks: Trace lead has been found in some lipsticks, with the FDA saying levels were not a safety concern and the CDC saying no blood lead level is safe. A 2021 study found fluorine, an indicator of PFAS, in many liquid lipsticks.

lead: Lipstick shade matching is the practice of choosing a lip colour to suit a person's skin tone, undertone, lip shape and overall look. People use it to make lips look more defined, to add colour and contrast to the lower face, and to balance the whole face, since it is a quick, removable change.[1][3]

Lipstick is a wax-and-oil colour product, and lip colour has been worn for thousands of years in many cultures.[1] Shade advice usually borrows from personal colour analysis, which sorts people by cool (bluer) or warm (yellower) undertone and often into four seasonal palettes, and applies the result to clothing and makeup.[3]

Controlled studies on how shade choice affects perceived attractiveness were not found. A 2026 study of Japanese Instagram influencers' lipstick classifications, as described by Wikipedia, found warm and cool categories matched measurable colour traits better than the four-season system.[3]

chain: Match shade to undertone and depth of colouring
Lips look defined and in balance with skin, eyes and hair
angle.text: A well-chosen shade changes lip colour and contrast immediately, and users pick it for how it relates to their skin tone and hair and eye colour. Lighter or deeper formulas also alter how full or defined the lips appear.

infobox: Waxes, oils, emollients, pigments and lake dyes[1]

paras: Lipstick is built on waxes such as beeswax, carnauba and candelilla, with oils, emollients, pigments and lake dyes providing colour. Matte formulas contain more filler agents such as silica, while glossy and sheer formulas contain more oil, and shimmer products may use mica or synthetic pearl particles. Pink shades are made by mixing white titanium dioxide with red pigments.[1]

Cosmetic colours have traditionally been matched to hair colour, eye colour, or both.[3] Seasonal colour analysis, described by Wikipedia, divides palettes into Winter, Spring, Summer and Autumn, with cool undertones leaning blue and warm undertones leaning yellow. It traces its roots to Chevreul (1839), Munsell (1905) and Johannes Itten (1961), and was popularised by Carole Jackson's Color Me Beautiful in 1980.[3]
Wikipedia notes that analysts need no standard training, and that a 2007 study of three systems found inconsistencies in how they used hue, saturation and value.[3]

Lip colour may date back about 5,000 years to Sumer and the Indus Valley, and the Chinese made beeswax lip products over a thousand years ago.[1] Guerlain is credited with the first commercial stick lipstick around 1884, and a swivel-up tube was patented in 1923.[1]

Fashionable shades have shifted over time: dark red in the 1920s, pale and novelty shades in the 1950s and 1960s, semi-matte in the 1990s, nude shades around 2014 and liquid mattes in 2015 and 2016.[1]

A 2007 Campaign for Safe Cosmetics study reported lead in 61% of 33 brands, and an FDA survey of 400 lipsticks in 2011 averaged 1.11 ppm with a maximum of 7.19 ppm. The FDA said such levels were not a safety concern because lipstick is lightly ingested, while the CDC states no blood lead level is considered safe.[1] A 2021 study found organic fluorine, an indicator of PFAS, in over half of 231 cosmetic products, with liquid lipsticks among those with the highest levels.[1]
A consumer-practice study of 360 women assessed how much lipstick is applied and how often, to support safety assessments.[2]

No studies found testing lipstick shade matching for perceived attractiveness or facial harmony. Related research covers cosmetic exposure and contaminants, and colour-classification studies of lipstick shades, rather than attractiveness outcomes.[2][3]

lore.intro: Shade matching appears in appearance communities as a low-cost, reversible way to alter perceived lip contrast and shape.

claims.claim: The right lipstick shade for your skin tone enhances lip shape and facial harmony.
claims.believers: Proponents say matching undertone and depth of colour makes lips look more defined and balances the face, and that lighter or darker shades can make lips look smaller or larger.
claims.experts: No controlled study of shade choice and perceived attractiveness was found; research on colour systems has examined consistency of the classification methods themselves.[3]

claims.claim: Warm or cool undertone determines the best shades
claims.believers: Colour analysts group people as cool (blue-leaning) or warm (yellow-leaning) and recommend palettes accordingly.[3]
claims.experts: A 2026 study cited by Wikipedia found warm and cool categories were more consistent with measurable lipstick colour traits than the four-season system.[3]
